title: Ibn Battuta: A Traveler of the World
summary: How Ibn Battuta of Tangier left home for Hajj in 1325, kept traveling for almost 30 years across Africa and Asia, and left behind the Rihla, a book historians still use.
poll: Traveling teaches you more than reading about places in books.

versions.title: Ibn Battuta
versions.text:
Long ago, a boy was born in Tangier. It is a town in Morocco. His name was Ibn Battuta.

At 21, he left home. He set out for Makkah. He went for Hajj. But he did not stop there. He went on and on. His journey took close to 30 years!

He went to lands near and far. He saw Egypt. He saw Syria. He went to India. He went to China. He went to Mali, too.

He rode with a caravan. That is a long line of camels. It went on hot sand. He sailed on a ship, too. Some trips were hard. There were storms. There were thieves. Once, a ship he was to sail on sank.

He knew the law. So in India, he was a judge. He helped end fights.

At last, he came back home. The king asked to hear his tale. A man wrote it all down. It made a big book. We still read it now. It tells us of the world long ago.

versions.title: Ibn Battuta: A Traveler of the World
versions.text:
About 700 years ago, a boy named Ibn Battuta was born in Tangier, a city in Morocco. As a young man, he studied the law.

In 1325, at the age of 21, he left home to make the pilgrimage to Makkah for Hajj. After the pilgrimage, however, he did not go home. He wanted to see more of the world, so he kept going. His journey lasted almost 30 years. He went about 120,000 kilometers in all.

Ibn Battuta visited lands that are now part of more than 40 countries. He saw Egypt, Syria, and Iraq. He sailed down the coast of East Africa. He went as far as India and China. Later, he crossed the Sahara Desert to Mali.

On land, he rode with caravans of camels and travelers who moved together for safety. At sea, he took long voyages on ships. These trips were often dangerous. He faced storms, robbers, and sickness. Once, a ship he planned to sail on sank in a storm. He lost most of what he owned.

Because he knew the law, Ibn Battuta worked as a judge for the sultan of Delhi in India. He also served as a judge in the Maldives, a group of islands in the Indian Ocean.

In 1354, he returned home for good. The sultan of Morocco asked him to share his adventures. A young scholar named Ibn Juzayy wrote down his stories in a book called the Rihla, which means "journey." Today, it is an important record that helps historians learn about the world long ago.

After completing the pilgrimage, however, he did not return, because he was deeply curious about the rest of the world. His journey eventually lasted almost 30 years and covered approximately 120,000 kilometers, a distance that few people before the modern age ever traveled.

He explored Egypt, Syria, and Iraq, sailed along the coast of East Africa, and traveled as far as India and China. Later, he crossed the enormous Sahara Desert to reach the wealthy kingdom of Mali in West Africa. versions.title: Ibn Battuta: A Traveler of the World
versions.text:
Approximately 700 years ago, a boy named Ibn Battuta was born in Tangier, a coastal city in Morocco, and as a young man he studied the law, which was a respected profession for an educated person during that period.

In 1325, at the age of 21, he departed from home to make the pilgrimage to Makkah for Hajj. After completing the pilgrimage, however, he did not return, because he was intensely curious about the remainder of the world. His journey eventually lasted almost 30 years and covered approximately 120,000 kilometers, a distance that few individuals before the modern era ever traveled.

Ibn Battuta visited territories that are now part of more than 40 countries, and consequently he experienced remarkably diverse cultures. He explored Egypt, Syria, and Iraq, sailed along the coast of East Africa, and ventured as far as India and China. Subsequently, he crossed the immense Sahara Desert to reach the prosperous kingdom of Mali in West Africa. Throughout his travels, he encountered rulers, merchants, and scholars, and he observed their cuisine, clothing, and customs with remarkable attentiveness.

On land, he journeyed with caravans of camels and travelers who moved together for protection, and at sea he undertook lengthy voyages aboard wooden vessels. These expeditions were frequently perilous, since he survived violent storms, attacks by bandits, and serious illness. On one memorable occasion, a ship he intended to board sank during a storm, and he lost nearly everything he possessed, including valuable gifts he had received from rulers.

Because of his legal training, Ibn Battuta was appointed as a judge by the sultan of Delhi in India, and he subsequently served as a judge in the Maldives, an archipelago in the Indian Ocean.

After returning home permanently in 1354, he was invited by the sultan of Morocco to dictate his recollections to a young scholar named Ibn Juzayy, who organized them into a book known as the Rihla, which means "journey." Today, this chronicle is an invaluable historical record that illuminates the fourteenth-century world, although some scholars question whether every detail is completely accurate. The work was completed in 1355, and its full title, which may be translated as A Gift to Those Who Contemplate the Wonders of Cities and the Marvels of Traveling, reflects the extraordinary curiosity that propelled its author across three continents.

His legacy endures in surprising locations: an international airport in Tangier and even a crater on the Moon commemorate his name.

keyWords.definition: a long trip from one place to another
keyWords.example: Our journey to the farm took four hours by car.

keyWords.definition: a group of people and animals, like camels, that travel together
keyWords.example: The caravan stopped at the well so the camels could drink.

keyWords.definition: a person whose job is to decide what is fair when people disagree
keyWords.example: The judge listened to both neighbors before she made a choice.

keyWords.definition: a large boat that carries people or goods across the sea
keyWords.example: The ship left the port early in the morning.

keyWords.definition: pages of writing put together for people to read
keyWords.example: I borrowed a book about space from the school library.

questions.stem: What is this article mostly about?
options: How to ride a camel safely in the desert
The history of the city of Tangier
The life and travels of Ibn Battuta
Why ships sank in storms long ago
questions.why: The article tells about Ibn Battuta, where he traveled, what happened on his trips, and the book about them.

wrong.A: Camels are mentioned, but the article does not teach how to ride one.
wrong.B: Tangier is where he was born, but the article is about his travels.
wrong.D: One ship sank, but that is only a small detail.

questions.stem: Why did Ibn Battuta first leave home?
options: To go to Makkah for Hajj
To work as a judge in India
To sell camels in Egypt
To sail a ship to China
questions.why: The article says he set out on a trip to Makkah for Hajj.

wrong.B: He worked as a judge later, but that is not why he left.
wrong.C: The article does not say he sold camels.
wrong.D: He went to China later in his journey.

questions.stem: How long did Ibn Battuta's journey last?
options: About one year
About ten years
About 100 years
Almost 30 years
questions.why: The article says his journey lasted almost 30 years.

wrong.A: His journey lasted much longer than one year.
wrong.B: Ten years is far too short.
wrong.C: No one could travel for 100 years.

questions.stem: The article says Ibn Battuta rode with a caravan. What is a caravan?
options: A big wooden ship that sails across the stormy sea
A group of camels and people who travel together
A book that tells about a long trip
A judge who helps people settle fights
questions.why: The article explains that a caravan is a long line of camels and people traveling together.

wrong.A: He sailed on ships at sea, but a caravan travels on land.
wrong.C: The book is the Rihla, not a caravan.
wrong.D: A judge is a person, not a group of travelers.

questions.stem: Why was Ibn Battuta able to work as a judge in India?
options: He was born in India.
He was very rich.
He knew the law.
He owned many camels.
questions.why: The article says he knew (had studied) the law, so he could work as a judge.

wrong.A: He was born in Tangier, Morocco.
wrong.B: The article does not say being rich made him a judge.
wrong.D: Camels had nothing to do with being a judge.

questions.stem: Which word best describes Ibn Battuta?
options: Lazy
Curious
Shy
Unkind
questions.why: After Hajj, he did not go home. He kept going to see more of the world, which shows he was curious.

wrong.A: Someone who travels for almost 30 years is not lazy.
wrong.C: He met many people and worked as a judge, so he was not shy.
wrong.D: He helped people settle fights, which is not unkind.

questions.stem: Why does the author tell about storms, thieves, and a ship that sank?
options: To teach readers how to build a strong ship
To explain how storms form over the sea
To prove that he never really left home
To show his trips could be dangerous
questions.why: These details show that his trips were hard and not always safe.

wrong.A: The article does not explain how to build ships.
wrong.B: The article does not explain how storms form.
wrong.C: The article says he traveled very far, so this is wrong.

questions.stem: Why do people still read Ibn Battuta's book today?
options: To learn about the world long ago
To find the road to Tangier
To learn how to become a judge
To look at its pictures of camels
questions.why: The book tells about the lands and people he saw, so readers learn what the world was like long ago.

wrong.B: The book is not a road map.
wrong.C: The book is about his travels, not how to become a judge.
wrong.D: The article does not say the book has pictures.

I told one problem he faced, using a fact from the article.

The sultan of Delhi wrote it from letters he received.
Merchants in Mali collected stories about him.
questions.why: The article says the sultan of Morocco invited him to dictate his recollections to the scholar Ibn Juzayy.

wrong.A: The book was written after he returned home, by Ibn Juzayy.
wrong.C: The sultan of Delhi employed him as a judge; he did not write the book.
wrong.D: The article does not mention merchants in Mali collecting stories.

questions.stem: Where did Ibn Battuta serve as a judge?
options: In Delhi and the Maldives
In Tangier and Makkah
In Mali and China
In Egypt and Syria
questions.why: The article states that he worked as a judge for the sultan of Delhi and later in the Maldives.

wrong.B: Tangier was his birthplace and Makkah his first destination.
wrong.C: He visited Mali and China but did not serve as a judge there.
wrong.D: He explored Egypt and Syria but was not a judge there.

questions.stem: The article says his expeditions were frequently perilous. What does perilous mean?
options: Slow and boring
Costly and rare
Full of danger
Short and easy
questions.why: The article follows the word with storms, bandits, illness, and a sinking ship, which show danger.

wrong.A: Nothing suggests the trips were boring.
wrong.B: Cost is not what the examples describe.
wrong.D: Journeys lasting years with storms were not short or easy.

questions.stem: Why did Ibn Battuta experience such diverse cultures?
options: He studied the languages of every nation before he left Morocco.
He visited lands that now belong to more than 40 countries.
He worked as a judge, which required moving to a new country every year.
He read books about other cultures while he stayed home in Tangier.
questions.why: Traveling through lands that are now more than 40 countries brought him into contact with many different peoples and customs.

wrong.A: The article does not say he studied languages first.
wrong.C: He was a judge in two places, not a new country every year.
wrong.D: He traveled himself rather than staying home to read.

questions.stem: Why might some historians question parts of the Rihla?
options: It was written in a language that nobody can read anymore today.
Ibn Battuta never actually left Morocco.
It describes only one city in great detail.
It was told from memory long after the events.
questions.why: The book was dictated as recollections after he returned home, years after many events, so some details may be mistaken.

wrong.A: Historians use the book today, so it can be read.
wrong.B: The article describes his travels across many lands.
wrong.C: The book covers many places, not one city.

questions.stem: What does naming an airport and a crater on the Moon after Ibn Battuta suggest?
options: His travels are still admired today.
He was the first person to study the Moon through a telescope.
He once claimed that he had traveled to the Moon himself.
Scientists believe he drew the first map of the Moon's craters.
questions.why: Naming places after someone honors them, which shows his legacy is still valued.

wrong.B: The article does not connect him to telescopes.
wrong.C: The article never says he claimed to visit the Moon.
wrong.D: The article does not say he mapped the Moon.

questions.stem: Why does the author mention that few people before the modern era traveled as far as Ibn Battuta?
options: To argue that modern travel is too dangerous
To explain why caravans used camels
To emphasize how unusual his achievement was
To show that he traveled mostly by airplane
questions.why: Comparing his distance with what others traveled highlights how remarkable his journey was.

wrong.A: The article does not discuss the dangers of modern travel.
wrong.B: Caravans are described elsewhere and for a different reason.
wrong.D: There were no airplanes in the fourteenth century.

HIGH.prompt: Ibn Battuta's Rihla is both an adventure story and a historical record. Using evidence from the article, explain why it is valuable today and why historians must still read it carefully.
checklist: I explained at least two reasons the Rihla is valuable, using evidence from the article.
I explained why historians read it carefully.
I used precise vocabulary from the article and organized my answer in clear paragraphs.
